Cycle-1 fix 7 is right about the king: Mercator's Praefatio in Atlantem names Atlas, a mythical king of Mauretania, a philosopher, mathematician and astronomer credited with the first globe (Wikipedia, Gerardus Mercator and Atlas (mythology); Crouch). Re-checking it found a new error: 'In 1595 Gerardus Mercator named his book' cannot be right, because Mercator died on 2 December 1594 in Duisburg (Britannica, Wikipedia). His son Rumold published the Atlas in 1595, after his death (LoC catalogue: 'left unfinished by the author … edited and published by his son, Rumold Mercator, in 1595'). Mercator chose the name; the book came out after he died. Wikipedia (Atlas): the word came to mean a collection of maps by the mid-17th century, which 'came to mean' covers. App-data note: eponyms-master.json's atlas story still says 'Mercator put a picture of Atlas holding up the world on the front … in 1595'. That is the claim cycle 1 corrected, so keep it off the Visitors' Book.
fix_text: To the ancient Greeks, Atlas was a Titan who held up the sky. Later tellings made him a wise king of Mauretania who studied the stars. Gerardus Mercator named his book of maps Atlas in that king's honour. It came out in 1595, the year after he died, and the word came to mean any book of maps.

Odyssey 11: the water was 'swallowed up and vanished away' whenever he stooped to drink (Theoi/Murray). Britannica: fruit hung above him 'that the wind kept out of reach'. Framed as what the ancient Greeks told. This is cycle-1 fix 9, applied.

Britannica and Theoi: Hypnos, the Greek god (personified spirit) of sleep. Etymonline: Braid coined neuro-hypnotism (1842) and hypnotism (1843) from Greek hypnos 'sleep'. Wikipedia: the hypn- terms were coined around 1820 by d'Hénin de Cuvillers and popularised by Braid; 'made the word popular' fits both. Braid was a Scottish surgeon, and Neurypnology (1843) called it 'nervous sleep'; he later conceded the term misled (Wikipedia). Britannica: hypnosis resembles sleep 'only superficially', so 'It isn't' is right. 'Hypnosis followed': Etymonline dates hypnosis to 1850 (coined as an alternative to hypnotism), M-W to 1876, both after hypnotism. This is cycle-1 fix 10, applied.

Britannica: Vulcan, Roman god of fire and metalworking (the forge). Etymonline: English volcano (1610s) from Italian vulcano 'burning mountain', from Latin Vulcanus. M-W: Italian vulcano from Spanish volcán, ultimately from Latin Volcanus; M-W's volcan entry routes the Spanish through Portuguese volcão. Either way the Italian and Spanish words come from his name, and the card does not pick a route. This is cycle-1 fix 11, applied.

Britannica: Frigg, Odin's wife; the Prose Edda ranks her highest of the Asynjur (Britannica Asynjur). Etymonline: 'queen of heaven'. M-W: Old English frīgedæg, from Frīg + dæg, a translation of Latin dies Veneris. Etymonline: Freya corresponds more closely to Venus. Wikipedia: whether Frigg and Freyja share a common origin is still debated. Every clause checks. This is cycle-1 fix 12, applied.
